statement: Five parcels P, Q, R, S and T all have different masses. P is heavier than Q, R is heavier than S, Q is heavier than S, and T is heavier than R. Which of these statements must be true?

choices.misconception: I lined up the clues in the order they were given and put P at the top, without noticing that T could be heavier still.
I stacked the chain P, Q on top of the chain T, R, S, as if everything in the first chain were heavier than everything in the second.
I assumed the parcel mentioned in the last clue, T, must be heavier than all the others in that part of the list.

choices.text: Q is the second lightest parcel.
choices.misconception: I placed Q just above S because they appear together in a clue, but R is also heavier than S and could be the one just above it.

hints: Draw the clues as arrows from heavier to lighter.
Ordering clues are easiest on a single line or as a diagram of arrows. A statement must be true only if every order that fits the clues makes it true, so look for one order that breaks it.
The clues form two chains, P above Q and T above R, both ending above S. Nothing links P with T or Q with R.

solutions.reliable: Draw arrows from heavier to lighter: P to Q, Q to S, T to R and R to S. Every other parcel is heavier than S, directly (Q and R) or through a chain (P through Q, T through R), so S must be the lightest. The other statements can all fail, because two different orders fit every clue. In the order T, R, P, Q, S (heaviest first), P is not the heaviest and Q is lighter than R. In the order P, Q, T, R, S, T is lighter than Q, and R, not Q, is the second lightest. The transferable idea: 'must be true' means true in every order that fits, so one counterexample is enough to rule a statement out.

whyOnTest: Partial orders test whether you see what the clues really fix; the traps are reading an order into the sequence the clues happen to be written in.
